overview.title: 📖 Overview: Species, Resemblance, and What May Be Eaten
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 6a–6b
overview.hebrewSource: זֶה הַכְּלָל: הַיּוֹצֵא מִן הַטָּמֵא — טָמֵא, וְהַיּוֹצֵא מִן הַטָּהוֹר — טָהוֹר
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf first nails down why only donkeys, among non-kosher animals, require redemption at all — comparing two independent derivations. It then works through a chain of dilemmas about cross-species births with partial resemblance to the mother, before turning to the mishna's kashrut rule that an offspring's status always follows its mother, not its own appearance. Rabbi Shimon dissents sharply regarding a camel born to a cow, which launches a wide-ranging discussion — including a famous aggadic aside about Shimon HaAmasoni's rule for expounding the word 'et' — into why the Torah needs a special verse to forbid a non-kosher animal's milk at all.

slides.title: 🐴 Excluding Horses and Camels From Redemption
slides.subtitle: Two independent routes to the same halakha

nodes.content: ❓ How do we know firstborn horses and camels need no redemption at all — not even with a non-lamb item?
📖 The doubled phrase 'firstborn of a donkey...firstborn of a donkey' teaches: donkeys alone are redeemed

columns.label: Rav Pappa's source
columns.content: 'From all your livestock take the males' (generalization) — 'ox, lamb, donkey' (detail). The generalization is limited to the detail: only these three species

columns.label: R' Yosei HaGelili vs. Rabbis
columns.content: Does 'firstborn' before 'donkey' interrupt the list (R' Yosei: donkey excluded), or does the extra 'and' fold it back in (Rabbis: donkey included)?

nodes.content: ✅ Rabbis: donkey needs its own split-and-rejoin because it carries a different TYPE of sanctity (value) than ox/lamb (inherent, offered on the altar)

slides.title: 🤔 Four Escalating Dilemmas: Partial Resemblance
slides.subtitle: How far does 'some characteristics of the mother' extend across species?

steps.content: 1️⃣ A cow gives birth to a donkey-like creature with some of its mother's traits. Does partial resemblance obligate it, even though cow and donkey carry different types of sanctity (inherent vs. value)?
2️⃣ Resolved from a baraita: yes — since both species carry some form of firstborn sanctity, partial resemblance is enough

3️⃣ Next: does this extend to a donkey giving birth to a horse-like creature (a species with no firstborn sanctity at all)? A second baraita turns out to address a different concern — that a donkey and horse both lack horns and have closed hooves, so one might mistake the offspring for merely an odd-colored donkey
4️⃣ Left open: whether a cow's horse-like offspring — combining kosher-vs-non-kosher and sanctified-vs-unsanctified — ever gets firstborn status through partial resemblance

callout.label: Method:
callout.text: The Gemara tests each new dilemma against existing baraitot, but not every baraita answers the question it initially seems to.

slides.title: 🐫 Kashrut Follows the Mother — Except According to Rabbi Shimon
slides.subtitle: A camel born to a cow: permitted or forbidden to eat?

boxes.title: The Rabbis (mishna's rule)
items: An offspring's kashrut always follows its mother's status, never its own appearance
Source: Leviticus 11:4 excludes only a kosher-looking creature born of a non-kosher mother
A camel born to a cow (kosher mother) would be permitted

boxes.title: Rabbi Shimon
items: The doubled verse 'camel...camel' (Leviticus 11:4, Deuteronomy 14:7) forbids both a camel born of a camel and one born of a cow
Also derives from the extra word 'et' (אֶת הַגָּמָל) that a camel's milk is forbidden

boxes.title: The Rabbis on Milk
items: They too use the doubled 'camel, camel' — but split it differently: one verse forbids the camel itself, the other its milk
They reject deriving new halakhot from the word 'et' altogether

slides.title: 📜 Shimon HaAmasoni and the Word 'Et'
slides.subtitle: A method of exegesis pushed until it hits a wall

lines.speaker: Shimon HaAm.
lines.text: I expound every extra word 'et' (אֶת) in the Torah to derive new halakhot — until I reached 'You shall fear et the Lord your God' (Deuteronomy 6:13). What could 'et' possibly add to the fear of God?

lines.speaker: Students
lines.text: But Rabbi — what becomes of everything you already derived from every earlier 'et'?

lines.speaker: Shimon HaAm.
lines.text: Just as I received reward for expounding, so I receive reward for withdrawing.

lines.speaker: R' Akiva
lines.text: Later I found the answer: that 'et' includes Torah scholars — one must revere them just as one reveres God.

callout.label: Why it matters here:
callout.text: This is exactly the dispute behind Rabbi Shimon's camel-milk derivation: he expounds 'et hagamal,' while the Rabbis, following Shimon HaAmasoni's retraction, do not.

slides.title: 🐑 Rabbi Shimon's Standard: 'Head and Most of the Body'
slides.subtitle: A stricter measure of resemblance, and whether it travels between contexts
rows: Firstborn status (e.g., a goat-like creature born to a ewe)
Rabbi Shimon: the offspring's head and majority of its body must resemble the mother — not just 'some characteristics'
'The firstborn of an ox' (Numbers 18:17) — must fully be that species
Eating a non-kosher-looking creature born to a kosher mother
Left an open dilemma: does the same strict 'head and majority' standard apply, or does any resemblance at all forbid it?
Unclear whether the firstborn standard and the eating standard are governed by the same measure

summary.principle: Only donkeys, among non-kosher animals, carry firstborn status, derived twice over from the Torah's language; and while an offspring's firstborn status and kashrut generally follow its resemblance to, and species of, its mother, Rabbi Shimon dissents sharply in the case of a camel born to a cow.

flowSteps.content: 🐴 Firstborn status limited to ox, lamb, and donkey — proven both from doubled verses and from a generalization-and-detail reading
🤔 Cross-species partial resemblance: obligates when both species carry some firstborn sanctity; unresolved when one carries none

columns.content: 🐫 Kashrut follows the mother (Rabbis) — but R' Shimon forbids a camel born of a cow, and its milk too
📜 Shimon HaAmasoni's 'et' method underlies that very dispute over the camel-milk verse

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: 'That which emerges from the non-kosher is non-kosher; that which emerges from the kosher is kosher' — the mother's status, not the offspring's looks, controls

quiz.q: According to Rav Pappa, how is it derived that only oxen, lambs, and donkeys — not other animals — carry firstborn status?
o: From a direct statement with no exegesis needed
From 'from all your livestock take the males' (generalization) followed by 'ox, lamb, donkey' (detail) — the generalization is limited to the detail
From the fact that these are the only domesticated animals
From a comparison to the Paschal offering
quiz.e: Rav Pappa applies the exegetical principle of generalization-and-detail: the general phrase 'all your livestock' is restricted to the specific animals listed afterward — ox, lamb, and donkey.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara resolve the dilemma of a cow giving birth to a donkey-like offspring that has some of its mother's characteristics?
o: It is never obligated in firstborn status
It is obligated, since both cow and donkey carry some form of firstborn sanctity
It depends on the offspring's color
The dilemma is left completely unresolved
quiz.e: A baraita resolves that since both species (cow and donkey) are subject to some type of firstborn sanctity, partial resemblance to the mother is sufficient to obligate the offspring.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Shimon, is a camel born to a cow permitted to be eaten?
o: Yes, since it follows its kosher mother's status
No — he holds the doubled verse 'camel, camel' forbids a camel born of a cow just as much as one born of a camel
Only if it lacks horns
The question does not apply to camels
quiz.e: Rabbi Shimon derives from the Torah stating 'camel' twice that both a camel born of a camel and one born of a cow are forbidden to eat, disagreeing with the mishna's general rule.

quiz.q: Why did Shimon HaAmasoni stop expounding the word 'et' (אֶת) throughout the Torah?
o: He ran out of time to complete his study
He reached 'You shall fear et the Lord your God' and could find nothing fitting to add to the fear of God
His students told him to stop
The Sages forbade the method entirely
quiz.e: Shimon HaAmasoni withdrew from his method when he reached this verse, since he could not identify what the extra 'et' should include alongside fearing God — until Rabbi Akiva later taught it includes Torah scholars.

quiz.q: According to the mishna's general rule (not Rabbi Shimon's view), what determines whether an offspring that looks like a different species may be eaten?
o: The offspring's own appearance alone
The mother's kashrut status, regardless of the offspring's appearance
Whichever ruling is more lenient
The species of the father
quiz.e: The mishna's rule, sourced from Leviticus 11:4, is that what emerges from a non-kosher animal is non-kosher and what emerges from a kosher animal is kosher — status follows the mother.
